title: Add an 'Estate' page to intentd that all intent-using Claudes on an estate can use to post status
objective: Give the host one live view of every Claude session on it: who it is, which project and node it stands in, whether it is busy, idle, in a heavy run or paused, its one-line WIP and its claims, with the host's load and the cargo and bats census. One source of truth on disk, a directory of session records under `~/.local/state/intent/estate/`, written by the sessions themselves through the hooks and the `intent estate` verbs; three renderers of it: intentd at `/estate/status` styled like top, `/estate` in the `intent explore` TUI beside `/projects`, and `intent estate status --json` for Claudes.
context: The estate is the host (rhadamanth, kovacs and gyges each its own), not a project; Intent, Devbin and Laksa are projects on it. Each project has a status surface already, the whiteboard, and what has no home is the layer above it: which sessions exist on the host, what each is doing, which heavy run holds the box. On 2026-10-24 that layer was run by hand over cross-session messages and a census script, and it vanished at every compact. intentd is one daemon per user with a web face and a registry of every project root on the host (ST0074), so it already knows the estate and renders none of it. State, not config: the records live under `~/.local/state/intent/estate/`, beside the daemon's own run dir, one writer per file, the readers never write, and the daemon reaps a record whose pid is dead. A session that is a whiteboard node does not copy its focus or claims into its record; the reader joins them from the project's store, so one fact has one home. The design is attached as `design.md`.

wps.title: The estate record and its doors: directory, versioned record, one reader, the estate verbs, MCP exposure, the reap rule
wps.objective:
One reader in `intentsvcs::estate` returns the host's estate as one serialisable value (schema `intent/estate-status@1`), and three verbs reach it: `intent estate status [--json]`, `intent estate wip "<line>"` (or `--clear`) and `intent estate prune`. Every renderer works from that value: the verb, intentd's `/op` (WP-02) and the TUI (WP-03).

The reader reads Claude Code's own `<claude dir>/sessions/<pid>.json` files and never writes them. A test pins the fields it relies on (pid, procStart, sessionId, cwd, name, status, startedAt, updatedAt) against a scrubbed real fixture. A file that lacks one of those fields is listed as unreadable, with the field named, never dropped. Claude Code's status is kept as found. A row's state is derived in this order: gone (a dead pid, or a pid whose start time is not the file's procStart, read with one `ps` call under the C locale and UTC) > paused > heavy > busy (any status but idle) > idle. A failed `ps` is reported as unreadable, never as every session gone. Liveness was measured on macOS; Linux is unmeasured until a kovacs session file is read.

The reader joins the project, node, focus and claims rather than storing them. The project is the one whose tree holds the session's cwd. A cwd in a git worktree folds to the main checkout through the git common dir, read-only, and the row says it is a worktree. Node, focus, claims and paused come from a narrow read of the node header of the board whose session id matches, under board schema @3.0 or @4.0, without opening any store; a board in another schema is unreadable, named.

Intent writes only what nothing else holds: `~/.local/state/intent/estate/<session-id>.json` (schema `intent/estate-session@1`), a WIP line for a session with no board. It is written whole by atomic rename, by that session alone. `prune` removes only those records for gone sessions, and never touches Claude Code's files.

Every error is typed and carries a remedy. `status` and `wip` are on MCP; `prune` is not.

The split: cc builds the intentsvcs side, ic the verbs' dispatch rows, help, exit codes and MCP rows.

wps.title: intentd serves /estate/status: watches the estate directory outside the ingest path, renders the live top-styled page with the host census
wps.objective: intentd answers the estate over the one shell document: the page's data call `{"op":"form","view":"/estate/status"}` returns `result: estate_status` carrying the reader's `intent/estate-status@1` JSON, /estate/status is a route in `shell.html` fed by `/op`, and the daemon renders no HTML for it (D56). The page is live and top-styled, laid out as the attached `estate-status-mockup.html` hv approved on 2026-10-24: one band across the top (the host block, the last hour as sparklines of the 1-minute load and the running slots, plan usage), then the queue, the lanes and the sessions, every panel a native `<details>` whose collapsed summary keeps a live one-line reading; it polls the reader every few seconds while open, so there is no watcher in this package and D20 keeps its two events. The daemon measures the host census itself on its tick: the load averages, one row per declared process class counting running processes attributed to the project whose tree holds each process's working directory, and a history ring; the classes are declared with `intent estate watch <class> <pattern>` and `intent estate unwatch <class>` as `census/watches/<class>.json`, nothing is built in, and the tick reaps gone sessions' WIP records (vc decision 73). Plan usage comes from the account's usage endpoint first, read through Claude Code's own Keychain item under Claude Code's own naming condition with no fallback between names, once per census tick after a status ask, and from `intent estate statusline` second, which a statusline step feeds the JSON it was handed (`printf '%s' "$input" | intent estate statusline || :`), printing `wrote:` on stderr and nothing on stdout; every failure is named in `usage.error`, never silent. `intent estate status --browser` opens the page. Decision 75: the rows of `estate status` are flat, and `watch`, `unwatch` and `statusline` are withheld from MCP with their reasons on the dispatch rows.

wps.title: The intent explore TUI: /estate beside /projects, on the same reader
wps.objective: The `intent explore` TUI gains /estate beside /projects, rendered from the same intentsvcs reader as the page and `intent estate status`, so the three renderers share one source of truth (PFIC, thin coordinator). The view shows the sessions table with each session's state (gone, paused, heavy, busy, idle), project and node, WIP or focus line with its age, claims and slots, and the host block with the census, and it shows the controller, the lanes and the queue once WP-04 fills those keys; until then it renders their empty values without branching. It re-reads on the explorer's refresh cadence, lists an unreadable session file as unreadable with the field named rather than dropping it, and reuses /projects' reader shape, measured first as the design asks. A `/estate` omnibox command opens it.

wps.title: Slots: a generic pool, ask, grant, start, release protocol on the estate, records beside the status records, capacity enforced by the tool, policy with the controlling Claude
wps.objective: A generic slot protocol on the estate with lanes and a named controller. The controller session, whichever session hv assigns, a dedicated one outside any project or a node inside one, takes control by writing `controller.json` (refused while a live holder's pid exists; a dead pid is succeeded) and declares lane types and lanes, each lane with a running capacity. Other sessions ask for a slot by lane type, the controller grants into a lane, denies or revokes, the holder starts and releases, and a grant over a lane's capacity is refused by the tool; policy beyond capacity stays with the controlling Claude. The records live beside the status records under `~/.local/state/intent/estate/slots/` (lanes, requests, the controller), each request a directory whose files are written one each by the acting party, so the state is the fold of the files and one writer per file holds. `slots wait` blocks a requester for its answer, `slots watch` streams state changes for the controller's monitor, and the UserPromptSubmit hook names pending asks to the controller. `intent estate init [<dir>]` renders a dedicated coordinator's working directory from Intent's own templates, contract and hook settings included, so the coordinator runs on Intent alone. The page and the TUI show the controller, every lane with its type, capacity, holders and queue, and each session's row shows the slots it holds.

criteria.text: One reader in intentsvcs returns the host's estate as one serialisable value, schema `intent/estate-status@1`, with every key present and typed from this package, so no renderer branches on a missing key; a key a later package fills carries the empty value of its declared shape until then.

The reader reads Claude Code's own session files under the config dir and never writes them; a test pins exactly the fields it relies on (pid, procStart, sessionId, cwd, name, status, startedAt, updatedAt), and a file lacking one is listed under `unreadable` with the field named, never dropped.

Project, node, focus and claims are joined, never stored: the project is the Intent project whose tree holds the session's cwd, a cwd in a git worktree folding to its main checkout; node, focus and claims come from the board whose recorded session id matches, read from the rendered `board.json` header under board schema 3.0 and 4.0 alike, and the reader opens no store.

`intent estate wip "<line>"` writes only `~/.local/state/intent/estate/<session-id>.json`, schema `intent/estate-session@1`, whole and by atomic rename, and prints `wrote:`; `intent estate prune` removes only Intent's own records for gone sessions and prints `removed:` per file; neither touches a Claude Code file.

A session whose pid is dead, or whose pid now belongs to a process started at a different time than its procStart (ctime via `ps` on macOS, clock ticks via `/proc/<pid>/stat` on Linux), renders as gone; a failed liveness read lists the file as unreadable and calls nobody gone; paused is a board's paused status and heavy is a running slot the session holds.

`estate status` and `estate wip` are exposed on MCP and `estate prune`, `estate watch`, `estate unwatch` and `estate statusline` are withheld, each dispatch row carrying its reason (decision 75), and `estate status --json` prints the reader's value unchanged.
Every error path of the estate verbs and the reader returns a typed error carrying a remedy, nothing is rescued and swallowed, and an unreadable session file is reported, not raised.

intentd answers the page's data call `{"op":"form","view":"/estate/status","root":...}` with `result: estate_status` carrying the reader's JSON; /estate/status is a route in the one shell document fed by `/op`, the daemon renders no HTML for it, and `/op` refuses without the bearer token as every op does.

The daemon's census tick measures the load averages and counts the running processes of each declared class, attributing each to the project whose tree holds its working directory and counting the rest as unattributed, keeps a history ring the page draws as the last hour, and reaps the WIP record of a gone session on the tick.

`intent estate watch <class> <pattern>` writes `census/watches/<class>.json` and changes the pattern on repeat, `intent estate unwatch <class>` removes it, each prints its `wrote:` or `removed:` line, the pattern is a regular expression matched against the process command line, and the census counts no class nobody declared.

Plan usage has a fallback: `intent estate statusline` reads the statusline JSON on stdin, writes the session record's rate limits, prints `wrote:` on stderr and nothing on stdout, exits 0 on an input with no rate_limits, and refuses non-JSON with a remedy; the page says which source it shows and how old it is, and every failure of either source is named in `usage.error`, never silent.

`intent estate status --browser` opens the page served by the running daemon, laid out as the attached `estate-status-mockup.html` hv approved on 2026-10-24 (the top band, the queue, the lanes, the sessions, each panel a native details element whose collapsed summary keeps a live reading), re-reading every few seconds while open.

criteria.text: Plan usage's primary source is the account's usage endpoint, read by intentd once per census tick after a status ask through Claude Code's Keychain item under Claude Code's own service-name condition (the suffixed name when CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR is set, the bare name when it is not, no fallback between them); the Keychain read failing, the endpoint unreached, a status other than 200 and an unparseable answer are each named in `usage.error`, and outside macOS the fallback is the source.

`intent explore` shows /estate beside /projects, rendered from the same intentsvcs reader as the page and the verb, with each session's state, project and node, line and its age, claims and slots, the host block with the census, and the controller, lanes and queue from the same keys the page reads, rendering their empty values without branching before WP-04 lands.
/estate re-reads on the explorer's refresh cadence, lists an unreadable session file as unreadable with the field named rather than dropping it, and `/estate` in the omnibox opens it.

`intent estate control take` writes `controller.json` beside the lanes with the session, its cross-session name and pid; a second take is refused while the holder's pid is alive, a dead pid allows a new take, `control release` ends it, and lane, grant, deny and revoke writes are accepted from the controller session only.

`intent estate slots lane open <lane> --type <type> --capacity <n>` writes `lanes/<lane>.json` and changes the capacity on repeat, `lane close <lane>` refuses while anything is granted in it, and a lane type is whatever the controller names, nothing being built in.

`slots ask <type> "<what>" [--lane <lane>]` writes `requests/<id>/ask.json` and prints the id; `grant <id> --lane <lane>`, `deny <id> "<why>"`, `revoke <id> "<why>"`, `start <id>` and `release <id>` each write their one file; a request's state is the fold of the files present (asked, granted, running, ended, denied, revoked); and a grant that would put the lane over its capacity, counting granted and running, is refused naming the count.

`slots wait <id>` blocks the requester until a grant or a denial lands, with a timeout; `slots watch` blocks and emits one line per state change under `slots/requests/` in the shape a Monitor consumes; and the UserPromptSubmit hook names the pending asks on the lane types the session controls.

`intent estate init [<dir>]` renders a dedicated coordinator's working directory from `lib/templates/estate/` through the same token expander as every root file, with AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md carrying the coordinator contract and `.claude/settings.json` wiring the `intent claude hook` lifecycle hooks, so a Claude Code session started there is the coordinator with only Intent installed.

The page, the TUI and `estate status` show the controller or NO CONTROLLER, every lane with its type, capacity, holders and the queue for its type, oldest first, and each session's row shows the slots it holds; a session holding a running slot in any lane reads as heavy.

# ST0086 design draft: the estate view

Written on 2026-10-24 from the rubber-duck between hv and vc. What is marked measured was measured; the rest is design to be measured before it is built.

## What it is

The estate is the host (rhadamanth, kovacs, gyges each its own). The estate view is a live top-styled table of every Claude session on the host: who it is, which project and node it stands in, whether it is busy, idle, in a heavy run or paused, its one-line WIP, its claims, and the host's load with a census of the process classes its controller declares. Three readers render one source of truth: intentd at /estate/status, the intent explore TUI at /estate, and `intent estate status --json` for Claudes.

## The source of truth

Presence and liveness are Claude Code's own session files, read and never written (hv's ruling, 2026-10-24). Claude Code writes `<config dir>/sessions/<pid>.json` for every session, where the config dir is `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or else `~/.claude` (measured on 2.1.310): `pid`, `procStart`, `sessionId`, `cwd`, `name` (the cross-session name), `status` (busy or idle), `startedAt`, `updatedAt` and `statusUpdatedAt` (epoch milliseconds), `messagingSocketPath`, `kind`, `entrypoint` and `version`. The format is not a published contract, so a reader test pins exactly the fields the reader relies on (pid, procStart, sessionId, cwd, name, status, startedAt, updatedAt), and a file that lacks one is shown as unreadable with the field named, never dropped. The reader lists `<pid>.json` only: Claude Code writes a `<pid>.<64 hex>.key` beside each session file (measured by cc on 2026-10-25, one pair per session), which the reader never opens or names, and an arm pins that it skips them by suffix. intentd runs today as a detached process whose parent is pid 1, not as a launchd job, and carries `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` in its environment (measured 2026-10-24), so the reader takes the config dir as a parameter and the daemon passes its own; a LaunchAgent intentd would not carry that variable, so its plist sets `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` under `EnvironmentVariables` to the value the sessions run with: without it the daemon reads `~/.claude/sessions` and asks the Keychain for the bare service name, which are another config's (WP-02).

Intent adds only what that file lacks, and joins most of it rather than storing it. Project root is the Intent project whose tree holds the session's cwd. Node, focus and claims come from the board whose recorded session id matches (`wb pickup` records it), read narrowly from that board's rendered `intent/whiteboard/<node>/board.json` header, under board schema 3.0 and 4.0 alike; the reader opens no store, since a read-write open of a peer project's store writes into it (cc's reading at WP-01, vc's ruling at its landing, 2026-10-24), and the header is the store's own tool-written render of those keys, so one fact keeps one home. Paused is a board's paused status. Heavy is a running slot the session holds in any lane, a light lane included (see Slots and lanes), and gone is a dead pid (see Cleanup); neither is written by anyone (vc's ruling, 2026-10-24). Intent writes per session only what nothing else holds, in `~/.local/state/intent/estate/<session-id>.json`: a schema version (pinned from day one, since the dev, opt and brew switch lets two intents share a host), the session id, a WIP line for a session with no board, the statusline's latest `rate_limits` where that fallback is in use (see Readers), and no stamp: the file's own mtime is its stamp, set by the atomic rename that writes it, so nothing asks a clock (D42). It is written whole by atomic rename by that session alone, with no locking; it is state, not config (intentd's socket already lives under `~/.local/state/intent/run`, measured).

## Writers

Presence needs no Intent hook: Claude Code keeps its own session file current. The explicit verbs: `intent estate wip "<line>"` (a session with no board), `intent estate prune` (Intent's own WIP records only), and the slot verbs below. MCP exposes `status` and `wip` because a repeat changes nothing; the slot verbs accumulate and stay CLI.

## Readers

One reader function in intentsvcs returns the joined table from the directory plus the stores it points at; the page, the TUI pane and the verb are renderers of it (PFIC, thin coordinator). The daemon adds the host census it measures itself, which retires vc's census script: the load, and a count of the running processes of each declared class, attributed to the project whose tree holds each process's working directory (a process in no known project counts as unattributed). The tool knows no process names, as it knows no lane names: the controller declares the classes, each a name and a pattern matched against the process's command line, with `intent estate watch <class> <pattern>` (and `intent estate unwatch <class>`), written as `census/watches/<class>.json` beside the slots. The verbs are flat, not `estate census watch`, because the spine builds a family and its verbs with no third level, and the subcommand-values idiom that would give one is the one the daemon family was moved off, because it puts two recoverabilities on one row (vc decision 75, 2026-10-25). `intent estate init` seeds the classes this host ran on 2026-10-24 (cargo and rustc, bats, mix and beam.smp, swift-build and xcodebuild); a project building with anything else adds its own. The page lists every declared class, those running with their count by project and those idle on one line, so a declared class never drops off the page (hv asked for this on 2026-10-24).

The page is not a second document (vc's ruling, 2026-10-24): under D56 the daemon serves one shell document, so /estate/status is a route in `shell.html`, fed by `/op` with the reader's JSON, and the daemon renders no HTML for it. The mockup attached as `estate-status-mockup.html` shows the page's layout and the raw record shapes it reads (census, controller, lanes, requests with one key per file present, sessions, and the boards the reader joins), from an inline sample that re-renders on a timer. hv approved its layout on 2026-10-24: one band across the top (the host block, the last hour as sparklines of the 1-minute load and the running slots, and plan usage), then the queue as its own panel, oldest first, then the lanes, then the sessions. Every panel is collapsible as a native `<details>`, with no script and no stored state, and a collapsed panel's summary line keeps a live one-line reading (the queue's waiting count and oldest age, usage percentages and whether the fallback is in use, the session tally), so folding a panel never hides activity; collapse all and expand all sit at the top. Rearranging panels is not in the mockup: if wanted, it is a per-viewer order kept in the browser, for WP-02 and WP-03 to decide. The sparklines need the daemon to keep a short in-memory ring of census samples (a minute apart, an hour long); it is not a record on disk and a restart starts it empty.

The reader's answer is `intent/estate-status@1`, and every key is present from WP-01, so a renderer never branches on a missing one; until the WP that fills a key lands, it carries the empty value of its declared shape, which is a valid instance of that shape, so filling it needs no schema bump (vc's ruling, 2026-10-24, since @1 has shipped nowhere). The keys: `schema`; `host` (null when `uname` fails); `version`; `taken_at`; `sessions`, each row carrying `session_id`, `name`, `pid`, `project` (`{root, name}` or null), `worktree`, `node`, `claude_status` (Claude Code's value verbatim), `state` (gone, paused, heavy, busy or idle), `started_at`, `updated_at`, `slots`, `claims`, `line`, `line_is_wip` and `line_at`; `unreadable`, each `{path, why, pid?}`; `census`, `{load, procs, history}`, empty arrays until WP-02, where `load` is the 1, 5 and 15 minute load averages, `procs` is one row per declared class, idle classes included so none drops off the page, `{class, count, projects: [{project, count}]}` with `project` the project's name or null for a process in no known project, and `history` is the in-memory ring, `[{at, load1, slots_running}]`, oldest first; `usage`, `{source, error, read_at, five_hour, seven_day, models}`, all null until WP-02, normalised by the reader so the page derives nothing: `source` is null when there is none, else `{kind, session_id}` with `kind` endpoint or statusline and `session_id` the reporting session's for the statusline, null for the endpoint; `error` names why the primary failed (the Keychain read, a status other than 200, an answer that will not parse), null when it did not; `read_at` is when the source was read; `five_hour` and `seven_day` are each `{percent, resets_at}` or null; and `models` is `[{name, percent, resets_at}]` from the endpoint's per-model caps, null when unavailable, which the statusline always is; and from WP-04 the three slot keys. `controller` is null when no session holds control, else `{session_id, name, pid, taken_at}`. `lanes` is `[{name, type, capacity, granted, running}]`, the last two counts of the requests granted and running in that lane. `queue` is `[{id, type, what, state, lane, asked_at, by}]`, every request not yet ended, denied or revoked, oldest first, where `id` is a ULID, `state` is the fold of its files (asked, granted or running), `lane` is null until a grant names one, and `by` is the requester's session id. Every stamp is ISO-8601 UTC with a `Z`.

Plan usage comes from two sources, the second a fallback (hv's ruling, 2026-10-24: "1 is the fallback. But I think 2 is worth it."):

- Primary, the account's usage endpoint, as the claudecodeusage menubar app reads it (measured from its source). intentd reads Claude Code's OAuth access token from the macOS Keychain with `/usr/bin/security find-generic-password -s <service> -w`, whose service is `Claude Code-credentials`, suffixed with `-` and the first eight hex digits of the SHA-256 of the config dir when `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is set and the bare name when it is not, which is Claude Code's own condition, with no fallback from one to the other: a fallback would read another config's token, and a test daemon run without the variable would reach the real Keychain; the value is JSON and the token is `claudeAiOauth.accessToken`. It then sends `GET https://api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/usage` with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and `anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20`, by spawning `/usr/bin/curl -sS --fail-with-body --max-time 10 -K -` at its absolute path with the URL and both headers in a config on its stdin, so the token is in no process's argv, and capturing the status and the body; intentd carries no TLS crate (vc decision 73). The answer carries `five_hour` and `seven_day` (`utilization`, `resets_at`), `seven_day_sonnet`, the per-model weekly caps in a `limits` array (`scope.model.display_name`, `percent`, `resets_at`) and `extra_usage`. intentd reads it at most once a census tick, never per page read, and only once a page has asked (the first ask wakes the tick), so a daemon nobody reads never touches the Keychain or the network; it keeps the last answer in memory. The token is never written, logged or sent anywhere but that endpoint. intentd reads the token by spawning `/usr/bin/security`, never through the Security framework itself: `/usr/bin/security` is on the item's access list, and that is the read measured silent (2026-10-24, the suffixed item, rc 0 in about a second with the token present and no dialog on screen, both as a detached process whose parent is launchd, which is how intentd runs today, and as a gui-domain LaunchAgent). A direct Security framework call from the intentd binary was not measured and would most likely prompt.
- Fallback, the statusline's `rate_limits` (measured on Claude Code 2.1.310): the JSON a session hands its statusline command carries an optional `rate_limits` with `five_hour` and `seven_day`, each `{used_percentage, resets_at}` in epoch seconds, for subscribers after the first API response, and no per-model figure. It is stdin to that command, not a file, so it reaches the estate only through a statusline step that writes the latest copy into the session's Intent record. The step (WP-02, vc decision 75): the statusline script pipes the JSON it was handed to `intent estate statusline`, with stdout untouched and the exit code ignored, `printf '%s' "$input" | intent estate statusline || :`, so a missing or broken intent never blanks the status bar. The verb prints its `wrote:` line on stderr and nothing on stdout, which is the status line; an input with no `rate_limits` writes and prints nothing.
- The failure path is named, never silent. When the Keychain read fails (no entry, access denied, a locked keychain), the endpoint answers anything but 200, or the answer will not parse, the page says which, shows the fallback's 5-hour and 7-day figures with their source and age, and marks per-model "unavailable" with the reason. With neither source it says "no source" and why. `usage.error` names each failure: no curl at `/usr/bin/curl`, the Keychain read, the endpoint unreached, a status other than 200 (with the status), and an answer that will not parse; a reading taken outside intentd names that the endpoint was not asked. The Keychain is macOS only: elsewhere the fallback is the source until another platform's credential store is measured.

## Cleanup

A session file whose pid is dead, or whose pid now belongs to a process started at a different time than its `procStart`, renders as gone. `procStart`'s form differs by OS (measured on both on 2026-10-24, Claude Code 2.1.310): on macOS it is UTC ctime, compared with `ps -o pid=,lstart=` under `LC_ALL=C` and `TZ=UTC` in one call for every pid; on Linux it is the kernel's start time in clock ticks since boot, compared with field 22 of `/proc/<pid>/stat`, an absent entry being gone. A failed liveness read is listed as unreadable and calls nobody gone. A session in another pid namespace, such as one in a container (its `pidDomain` names the namespace), reads as gone, since the reader does not cross namespaces. Claude Code's files are never deleted by Intent; the daemon reaps only Intent's own WIP record for a gone session on its next tick, and `intent estate prune` does the same where no daemon runs. A live pid with an old `updatedAt` renders as idle with its age and is never reaped. A slot whose holder is gone renders as orphaned until its controller revokes it; a controller whose pid is dead leaves its record orphaned, and the next `control take` succeeds it. Readers never write.

## Slots and lanes

A generic way for one session to control how much of something runs at once and for others to ask for a share. Nothing in the tool knows what a lane is for; the names below (heavy, light, kovacs) are the ones 2026-10-24 ran by hand and are examples, not a fixed set.

- A lane type is a class the controller declares (heavy, light, kovacs). A lane is an instance of a type with its own running capacity: `intent estate slots lane open <lane> --type <type> --capacity <n>`; the same verb changes the capacity, and `lane close <lane>` ends it when nothing is granted in it. How many lanes, of which types, with what capacity, is the controller's call. On 2026-10-24 that was two heavy lanes of capacity one on the Mac (cargo, bats), one light lane beside bats, and one kovacs lane.
- A request asks by type, and may name a lane: `intent estate slots ask <type> "<what>" [--lane <lane>]` returns an id and queues it. Queued is per type. `slots wait <id>` blocks the requester until a grant or a denial lands, with a timeout.
- The controller: `grant <id> --lane <lane>`, `deny <id> "<why>"`, `revoke <id> "<why>"`. A grant that would put the lane over its capacity, counting granted and running, is refused and names the count; the controller raises the capacity if it means it. Which request goes first is the controller's judgement, never the tool's.
- The holder: `start <id>` and `release <id>`. `status` shows every lane with its type, capacity, holders and the queue for its type, and each session's row shows the slots it holds.
- The files are the protocol, under `~/.local/state/intent/estate/slots/`: `lanes/<lane>.json` written by the controller; each request a directory `requests/<id>/` holding `ask.json` from the requester, `grant.json` (naming the lane) or `deny.json` from the controller, `start.json` and `end.json` from the holder, `revoke.json` from the controller. A request belongs to no lane until granted. Its state is the fold of the files present (asked, granted, running, ended, denied, revoked), so one writer per file holds, no lock exists, and the readers read it like the session files.
- Learning without polling: `wait` for the requester; for a controller, the UserPromptSubmit hook names the pending asks on the lane types its session controls, the way it injects project context today.
- Out of the first cut: priorities, and any policy beyond capacity. Succession is by pid liveness only (see The coordinator).

## The coordinator

The controller is whichever session hv assigns to manage the workload: a dedicated session that stands in no Intent project, or a node inside one. The protocol treats both the same and names the role by a record instead of relying on a volunteer, which is what 2026-10-24 did.

- Control is a record: `intent estate control take` writes `controller.json` beside the lanes, one per host, with the session, its cross-session name and pid; `control release` ends it. A second take is refused while the holder's pid is alive; a dead pid leaves the record orphaned and a new take is allowed, which is the whole of succession in the first cut. Lane, grant, deny and revoke writes are accepted from the controller session only.
- The page and `status` show the controller at the top, or NO CONTROLLER, in which case asks queue and nothing is granted.
- Waking it: `intent estate slots watch` blocks and emits one line per state change under `slots/requests/` (asked, started, released), the shape a Monitor consumes, and the coordinator's contract arms it at session start. Requesters have `wait`, the coordinator has `watch`, and the UserPromptSubmit hook injects the pending asks on top.
- A dedicated coordinator stands in no project and has no node, so its WIP line is set directly; a project node that takes control keeps its project and node, and the reader joins its focus as for any node.
- All of it inside Intent, nothing else needed: `intent estate init [<dir>]` renders a dedicated coordinator's working directory from Intent's own templates (`lib/templates/estate/`, through the same token expander as every root file): its AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md carrying the coordinator contract (take control at session start, arm `slots watch` under a monitor, judge asks against lane capacity and the estate view, release control at session end), and `.claude/settings.json` wiring the same `intent claude hook` lifecycle hooks a project gets. A Claude Code session started in that directory is the coordinator with only Intent installed. A project node that is assigned control follows the same contract, carried to it by the hook injection.

Cross-project announce; federation of estates across hosts (kovacs on rhadamanth's page); slot policy beyond capacity; anything a sleeve or dotfiles framework would add on top, since the coordinator runs on Intent alone.
